questions.prompt: Which of the following is a TRUE statement about transient ischemic attacks (TIAs)?
options: They usually cause necrosis and permanent brain damage.
They may be caused by rupture of an aneurysm or a damaged artery.
They can warn of potential cerebrovascular accidents
questions.suggestedLabel: D. They can warn of potential cerebrovascular accidents
questions.suggestedRationale: TIAs are brief ischemic events that resolve but warn of a possible stroke.

questions.prompt: One function of the somatic nervous system that is not performed by the autonomic nervous system is conduction of impulses:
options: between the brain and spinal cord
questions.suggestedLabel: C. to skeletal muscles.
questions.suggestedRationale: The somatic nervous system uniquely supplies skeletal muscle; the ANS supplies involuntary effectors.

questions.prompt: The composition of cerebrospinal fluid is
options: a plasma-like liquid with glucose, salts, and proteins
a heavy mucous solution with dissolved salts, glucose, and urea
questions.suggestedLabel: C. a plasma-like liquid with glucose, salts, and proteins
questions.suggestedRationale: CSF is a clear, plasma-like fluid containing glucose and salts, with very little protein.

questions.prompt: Through what area does the cerebrospinal fluid circulate around the brain and spinal cord?
options: Between the double layers of the dura mater
questions.suggestedLabel: C. In the subarachnoid space
questions.suggestedRationale: CSF circulates in the subarachnoid space around the brain and cord.

questions.prompt: Neurons that carry impulses away from the CNS are called
questions.suggestedLabel: C. efferent neurons.
questions.suggestedRationale: Efferent (motor) neurons carry impulses away from the CNS.

questions.prompt: Which of the following applies to the corticospinal tract?
options: The nerve fibers conduct sensory impulses.
It is a pyramidal tract for efferent impulses.
questions.suggestedLabel: D. It is a pyramidal tract for efferent impulses.
questions.suggestedRationale: The corticospinal tract is a pyramidal motor (efferent) pathway.

questions.prompt: What is a major function of the limbic system?
options: Required for logical thinking, reason, and decision making
Responsible for artistic and musical talents
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Determines emotional responses
questions.suggestedRationale: The limbic system is the main driver of emotional responses.

questions.prompt: What does a vegetative state refer to?
options: Depression of the reticular activating system (RAS) and inability to initiate action
Loss of awareness and intellectual function but continued brainstem function
Continuing intellectual function but inability to communicate or move
Disorientation and confusion with decreased responsiveness
questions.suggestedLabel: B. Loss of awareness and intellectual function but continued brainstem function
questions.suggestedRationale: A vegetative state is loss of awareness and cognition with preserved brainstem function.

questions.prompt: Which of the following conditions is NOT part of the criteria for a declaration of “brain death”?
questions.suggestedLabel: D. Presence of any head injury
questions.suggestedRationale: Brain death requires no EEG activity, no reflexes, and no spontaneous respirations—not merely the presence of a head injury.

questions.prompt: What is the best definition of aphasia?
options: The inability to comprehend or express language appropriately
Loss of the visual field contralateral to the area of damage
The inability to articulate words clearly
questions.suggestedLabel: A. The inability to comprehend or express language appropriately
questions.suggestedRationale: Aphasia is impaired comprehension or expression of language; unclear articulation is dysarthria.

questions.prompt: Neurons are specialized for the conduction of impulses, whereas neuroglia
options: All of the above are correct
questions.suggestedLabel: A. support nerve tissue.
questions.suggestedRationale: Neuroglia support and protect neurons rather than conduct impulses.

questions.prompt: What is an early indicator of increased intracranial pressure?
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Decreasing responsiveness
questions.suggestedRationale: Decreasing responsiveness (level of consciousness) is an early sign of rising ICP; papilledema and fixed pupils come later.

questions.prompt: What is the typical change in blood pressure in a patient who has increased intracranial pressure?
options: Systolic and diastolic pressures decreasing proportionately
questions.suggestedLabel: D. Increasing pulse pressure
questions.suggestedRationale: Cushing change is a widening pulse pressure (rising systolic, relatively low diastolic).

questions.prompt: The largest category of primary malignant brain tumors that arise from cells in the central nervous system (CNS) are called
questions.suggestedLabel: A. gliomas.
questions.suggestedRationale: Gliomas are the largest group of primary malignant CNS tumors.

questions.prompt: Which of the following causes papilledema?
options: Increased pressure of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) at the optic disc
questions.suggestedLabel: A. Increased pressure of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) at the optic disc
questions.suggestedRationale: Papilledema is swelling of the optic disc from transmitted high CSF pressure.

questions.prompt: The reticular activating system:
options: programs for fine repetitive motor movements.
affects the positioning of the head to improve hearing
questions.suggestedLabel: B. maintains wakefulness.
questions.suggestedRationale: The reticular activating system maintains wakefulness and alertness.

questions.prompt: What is the effect of an enlarging brain abscess on cardiovascular activity?
options: Increased heart rate and systemic vasodilation
Low blood pressure and irregular heart and respiratory rates
Systemic vasoconstriction and slower heart rate
Immediate depression of the cardiac control centers
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Systemic vasoconstriction and slower heart rate
questions.suggestedRationale: Rising ICP triggers the Cushing response: systemic vasoconstriction and a slower heart rate.

questions.prompt: As intracranial pressure rises, the pupil of the eye, ipsilateral to the lesion, becomes dilated and unresponsive to light because of pressure on the
options: peripheral nervous system (PNS) fibers in cranial nerve III.
sympathetic nervous system (SNS) nerve to the eye.
questions.suggestedLabel: B. peripheral nervous system (PNS) fibers in cranial nerve III.
questions.suggestedRationale: Ipsilateral pupil dilation comes from compression of parasympathetic fibers in CN III.

questions.prompt: The sympathetic division of the autonomic nervous system:
options: mobilizes energy in times of need.
is innervated by cell bodies from T1 through L2.
is innervated by cell bodies located in the cranial nerve nuclei
questions.suggestedLabel: D. Both A and B
questions.suggestedRationale: Sympathetic outflow is thoracolumbar (T1–L2) and mobilizes energy for 'fight or flight.'

questions.prompt: The parasympathetic division of the autonomic nervous system:
options: Both a and b are correct.
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Both a and b are correct.
questions.suggestedRationale: Parasympathetic nerves conserve energy and have short postganglionic fibers; paravertebral ganglia are sympathetic.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements is TRUE about malignant brain tumors?
options: Most brain tumors arise from malignant neurons.
Primary brain tumors rarely metastasize outside the CNS.
The blood-brain barrier prevents secondary brain tumors.
Brainstem tumors do not manifest signs until they are quite large.
questions.suggestedLabel: B. Primary brain tumors rarely metastasize outside the CNS.
questions.suggestedRationale: Primary brain tumors rarely spread outside the CNS.

questions.prompt: Why are focal or generalized seizures sometimes an early indication of a brain tumor?
options: Surrounding inflammation stimulates neurons to discharge spontaneously.
Malignant tumors cause alkalosis, exciting the CNS.
Systemic effects of the brain tumor may cause seizures.
Metabolic effects of cancer change blood chemistry to trigger seizures.
questions.suggestedLabel: A. Surrounding inflammation stimulates neurons to discharge spontaneously.
questions.suggestedRationale: Irritation and inflammation around a tumor can make nearby neurons fire and produce seizures.

questions.prompt: What is the probable source of an embolus causing a cerebrovascular accident (CVA)?
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Common carotid artery
questions.suggestedRationale: An arterial embolus to the brain commonly originates in the carotid (or left heart)—not the venous system.

questions.prompt: Collateral circulation is most likely to be present when a CVA results from
questions.suggestedLabel: C. atherosclerosis.
questions.suggestedRationale: Slow atherosclerotic narrowing allows time for collateral circulation to develop.

questions.prompt: All of the following apply to CVA EXCEPT
options: the common cause is an atheroma with thrombus.
maximum necrosis and infarction develop within several hours of onset.
warning signs may appear with partial obstruction of the artery.
increasing neurological deficits usually develop during the first few days.
questions.suggestedLabel: B. maximum necrosis and infarction develop within several hours of onset.
questions.suggestedRationale: Infarction and deficits often evolve over 1–2 days, so 'maximum necrosis within several hours' is the exception.

questions.prompt: Signs and symptoms of a stroke depend upon
options: location of obstruction, size of artery, and area affected.
duration of the blockage, distance from the heart, and type of obstruction.
health of the victim, area affected, and collateral circulation.
size of the obstruction, condition of the heart, and duration of blockage.
questions.suggestedLabel: A. location of obstruction, size of artery, and area affected.
questions.suggestedRationale: Stroke signs depend on the artery involved, its size, and the brain territory it supplies.

questions.prompt: An individual shows flexion in upper extremities and extension in lower extremities. This is:
questions.suggestedLabel: A. decorticate posturing.
questions.suggestedRationale: Decorticate posturing is flexion of the arms with extension of the legs.

questions.prompt: Cerebral death:
options: is death of the brain stem.
questions.suggestedLabel: B. permits normal internal homeostasis.
questions.suggestedRationale: Cerebral (neocortical) death can leave the brainstem able to maintain basic internal homeostasis.

questions.prompt: Precipitating causes of seizure include all of the following except:
options: e. All of the above are correct
questions.suggestedLabel: C. hyperglycemia.
questions.suggestedRationale: Hypoglycemia, not hyperglycemia, is the typical metabolic trigger for seizures; meningitis, stroke, and fever can precipitate them.

questions.prompt: Postictal sleeping can be seen in what type of seizure
questions.suggestedLabel: D. tonic-clonic
questions.suggestedRationale: A postictal sleep is typical after a tonic-clonic seizure.

questions.prompt: Alzheimer disease:
options: can be caused by increased cerebral levels of acetylcholine.
is most prevalent as a late-onset dementia.
e. All of the above are correc
questions.suggestedLabel: B. is most prevalent as a late-onset dementia.
questions.suggestedRationale: Alzheimer disease is most often late-onset; plaques and tangles also occur, but acetylcholine is decreased, not increased, so 'all of the above' is wrong.

questions.prompt: Which statement is not true regarding increasing intracranial pressures?
options: The blood volume in the vessels increases.
Brain tissue shifts from the compartment of greater pressure to one of lesser pressure.
e. Both b and c are correct.
questions.suggestedLabel: A. Accumulating CO2 causes vasoconstriction.
questions.suggestedRationale: CO2 dilates, rather than constricts, cerebral vessels, so that statement is not true.

questions.prompt: Intellectual function is impaired in the dementing process. Which intellectual function is not impaired?
options: e. All of the above functions are impaired
questions.suggestedLabel: E. e. All of the above functions are impaired
questions.suggestedRationale: Dementia can impair new and old memory, abstraction, and language—so none of those functions is reliably spared.

questions.prompt: In an automobile accident, an individual’s forehead struck the windshield. The coup/contrecoup injury would be in the
questions.suggestedLabel: B. frontal/occipital region.
questions.suggestedRationale: A forehead (coup) impact produces a frontal injury and a contrecoup injury at the occipital pole.

questions.prompt: An Injury of the cervical cord may be life threatening because of:
options: loss of bladder and rectal control.
questions.suggestedLabel: E. e. diaphragmatic impairment
questions.suggestedRationale: High cervical cord injury can paralyze the diaphragm (C3–C5) and stop breathing.

questions.prompt: Autonomic dysreflexia is characterized by all of the following except:
options: stimulation of sensory receptors below the level of the cord lesion.
precipitation because of a distended bladder or rectum
questions.suggestedLabel: A. hypotension.
questions.suggestedRationale: Autonomic dysreflexia causes hypertension, not hypotension.

questions.prompt: TIAs are:
options: unilateral neurologic deficits that slowly resolve.
generalized neurologic deficits that occur a few seconds every hour.
focal neurologic deficits that develop suddenly, last more than an hour, and clear without evidence of infarction.
neurologic deficits that slowly evolve or develop
questions.suggestedLabel: C. focal neurologic deficits that develop suddenly, last more than an hour, and clear without evidence of infarction.
questions.suggestedRationale: Best match: sudden focal deficits that clear without infarction (modern definitions usually limit TIA duration to under an hour, so the wording is slightly off).

questions.prompt: Manifestations of subarachnoid hemorrhage include which of the following? (More than one answer may be correct)
questions.suggestedLabel: A. a stiff neck
questions.suggestedRationale: Stiff neck is a classic SAH sign; Kernig sign can also occur, but the form offered no combined choice.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements about berry aneurysms in the brain is NOT true?
options: They usually develop at points of bifurcation in the circle of Willis.
They are usually asymptomatic for many years.
Following rupture, blood appears in the subarachnoid space.
questions.suggestedLabel: C. CSF remains free of blood.
questions.suggestedRationale: After rupture, blood enters the CSF, so it is not true that CSF 'remains free of blood.'

questions.prompt: What are significant signs of acute bacterial meningitis?
options: Severe headache, nuchal rigidity, and photophobia
Fatigue and lethargy, fever, and anorexia
Focal signs, such as progressive paralysis in a limb
Ascending paralysis beginning in the legs
questions.suggestedLabel: A. Severe headache, nuchal rigidity, and photophobia
questions.suggestedRationale: Acute bacterial meningitis classically presents with severe headache, neck stiffness, and photophobia.

questions.prompt: All of the following apply to tetanus infection EXCEPT
options: it is caused by an anaerobic, spore-forming bacillus.
the exotoxin causes strong skeletal muscle spasms.
death usually results from respiratory failure.
signs of fever, vomiting, stiff neck, and paralysis.
questions.suggestedLabel: D. signs of fever, vomiting, stiff neck, and paralysis.
questions.suggestedRationale: Fever, vomiting, stiff neck, and paralysis describe meningitis, not tetanus.

questions.prompt: In cases of Guillain-Barré syndrome, what does the pathophysiology include?
options: Damage and loss of function in the motor neurons of the spinal cord and medulla
Encephalopathy, with disorientation, headache, and coma
Infection and inflammation of the motor cortex
Inflammation and demyelination of peripheral nerves, leading to ascending paralysis
questions.suggestedLabel: D. Inflammation and demyelination of peripheral nerves, leading to ascending paralysis
questions.suggestedRationale: GBS is inflammatory demyelination of peripheral nerves with ascending paralysis.

questions.prompt: Following a head injury, what is the most likely cause of secondary damage to the brain?
options: Tearing of blood vessels as the brain rotates across the inside of the skull
questions.suggestedLabel: A. Hematoma or infection
questions.suggestedRationale: Secondary brain injury after trauma commonly comes from hematoma, infection, or ischemia/hypoxia; hematoma or infection is the listed pair.

questions.prompt: Vertebral fractures are classified as
questions.suggestedLabel: A. simple, compression, wedge, dislocation.
questions.suggestedRationale: Vertebral fractures are grouped as simple, compression, wedge, or dislocation.

questions.prompt: How does the heart rate change as intracranial pressure increases?
questions.suggestedLabel: A. Rate decreases
questions.suggestedRationale: As ICP rises, heart rate typically falls (Cushing bradycardia).

questions.prompt: Which type of cerebrovascular accident (CVA) has the poorest prognosis?
questions.suggestedLabel: B. Hemorrhagic CVA
questions.suggestedRationale: Hemorrhagic strokes generally have the poorest prognosis of the CVA types.

questions.prompt: What are the significant early signs of a ruptured cerebral aneurysm?
options: Severe headache, nuchal rigidity, and photophobia
questions.suggestedLabel: B. Severe headache, nuchal rigidity, and photophobia
questions.suggestedRationale: A ruptured aneurysm presents with sudden severe headache, nuchal rigidity, and photophobia.

questions.prompt: With regard to meningitis, choose the correct combination of microbe and the age group commonly affected.
questions.suggestedLabel: C. N. meningitides: children and youth
questions.suggestedRationale: Neisseria meningitidis typically affects children and adolescents/young adults.

questions.prompt: Which signs are indicative of post-polio syndrome?
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Progressive fatigue and weakness
questions.suggestedRationale: Post-polio syndrome is later progressive fatigue and weakness, not a new acute paralysis.

questions.prompt: Which of the following does NOT apply to Reye’s syndrome?
options: There is no permanent damage in the body.
It is precipitated by a combination of viral infection and administration of acetylsalicylic acid (ASA).
questions.suggestedLabel: A. There is no permanent damage in the body.
questions.suggestedRationale: Reye syndrome can leave lasting brain and liver injury, so 'no permanent damage' does not apply.

questions.prompt: The primary reason for seizures frequently occurring with head injuries is
options: presence of blood irritates the neurons
otorrhea or rhinorrhea changes intracranial pressure.
questions.suggestedLabel: A. presence of blood irritates the neurons
questions.suggestedRationale: Blood in contact with the cortex after head injury irritates neurons and can trigger seizures.

questions.prompt: Common manifestations of rabies infection include
options: headache, foaming at the mouth, and difficulty swallowing.
decreased sensitivity to sound and touch.
questions.suggestedLabel: A. headache, foaming at the mouth, and difficulty swallowing.
questions.suggestedRationale: Rabies causes hydrophobia, dysphagia, and foaming at the mouth, often with headache.

questions.prompt: Tetanus infection is:
options: It is caused by a virus.
Infection usually develops in deep puncture wounds.
It causes flaccid skeletal muscles, impairing mobility.
It affects peripheral nerves initially in the legs and feet.
questions.suggestedLabel: B. Infection usually develops in deep puncture wounds.
questions.suggestedRationale: C. tetani typically infects deep, anaerobic puncture wounds.

questions.prompt: Which of the following impairments results from infection by the polio virus?
options: Pain and paresthesia in a cranial nerve or dermatome
Loss of motor and sensory function in the peripheral nerves
Loss of function of motor neurons of the spinal cord and medulla
questions.suggestedLabel: D. Loss of function of motor neurons of the spinal cord and medulla
questions.suggestedRationale: Poliovirus destroys anterior-horn and medullary motor neurons.

questions.prompt: In cases of noncommunicating hydrocephalus, why does excess cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) accumulate?
options: Absorption of CSF through the arachnoid villi is impaired.
Excessive amounts of CSF are produced in the ventricles.
An obstruction is present in the aqueduct of Sylvius or other channel.
Flow around the spinal cord is blocked.
questions.suggestedLabel: C. An obstruction is present in the aqueduct of Sylvius or other channel.
questions.suggestedRationale: Noncommunicating hydrocephalus is a blockage in the ventricular pathways (for example, the aqueduct).

questions.prompt: All of the following are typical signs of hydrocephalus in the neonate EXCEPT
options: eyes turned downward with sclerae showing above the pupils. (sunset sign)
questions.suggestedLabel: B. vomiting, headache, and paralysis.
questions.suggestedRationale: Neonates show an enlarging head and sunset eyes; headache and paralysis are more typical in closed-skull older patients.

questions.prompt: Myelomeningocele is
options: asymptomatic failure of the posterior spinous processes of the vertebrae to fuse.
herniation of the meninges through a vertebral defect.
herniation of the meninges, CSF, and spinal cord or nerves through a vertebral defect.
herniation of brain tissue through a defect in the cranium
questions.suggestedLabel: C. herniation of the meninges, CSF, and spinal cord or nerves through a vertebral defect.
questions.suggestedRationale: Myelomeningocele herniates meninges, CSF, and spinal cord or nerves through a vertebral defect.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is characteristic of generalized seizures?
options: The localization of the seizure activity
The uncontrolled discharge of neurons in both hemispheres
Seizures that persist for several hours
Loss of consciousness and all motor function
questions.suggestedLabel: B. The uncontrolled discharge of neurons in both hemispheres
questions.suggestedRationale: A generalized seizure is bilateral, uncontrolled discharge of both hemispheres.

questions.prompt: From the following, choose the two events (in correct sequence) that immediately follow the aura during a tonic-clonic event:
options: Prodromal signs, then the clonic stage
Clonic stage, then the tonic stage
Loss of consciousness, then the tonic stage
Loss of consciousness and cessation of respiration
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Loss of consciousness, then the tonic stage
questions.suggestedRationale: After the aura comes loss of consciousness and then the tonic phase.

questions.prompt: What does the clonic stage of a seizure consist of?
options: A sudden strong skeletal muscle contraction and rigidity of trunk and limbs
A cry and contraction of abdominal and thoracic muscles
Alternating contractions and relaxation of skeletal muscles
Cessation of all skeletal muscle activity
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Alternating contractions and relaxation of skeletal muscles
questions.suggestedRationale: The clonic phase is rhythmic alternating contraction and relaxation of skeletal muscle.

questions.prompt: How would a seizure consisting of bizarre or inappropriate activity be classified?
questions.suggestedLabel: B. Psychomotor seizure
questions.suggestedRationale: Bizarre or inappropriate automatic behavior typifies a psychomotor (complex partial) seizure.

questions.prompt: Which statement does NOT apply to the pathophysiology of multiple sclerosis?
options: It affects the brain, spinal cord, and cranial nerves
It affects motor, sensory, and autonomic fibers
Progressive random degeneration of peripheral nerves
questions.suggestedLabel: D. Progressive random degeneration of peripheral nerves
questions.suggestedRationale: MS is a CNS demyelinating disease; it does not randomly degenerate peripheral nerves.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are common early signs of multiple sclerosis?
options: Paralysis of the lower body, impaired cognitive function
Areas of numbness, weakness in the legs, visual problems
Sensory deficit in the legs and trunk, memory loss, urinary incontinence
questions.suggestedLabel: B. Areas of numbness, weakness in the legs, visual problems
questions.suggestedRationale: Early MS often brings patchy numbness, leg weakness, and visual disturbance.

questions.prompt: What is the pathophysiological change in Parkinson’s disease?
options: Degeneration of motor fibers in the pyramidal tracts
Excess secretion of stimulatory neurotransmitters in the CNS
Degeneration of the basal nuclei with a deficit of dopamine
Deficit of acetylcholine and degeneration of the motor cortex in the frontal lobe
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Degeneration of the basal nuclei with a deficit of dopamine
questions.suggestedRationale: Parkinson disease is degeneration of basal nuclei (substantia nigra) with dopamine deficiency.

questions.prompt: In which type of neuron is progressive degeneration occurring with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)?
options: Motor, sensory, and autonomic system neurons
questions.suggestedLabel: B. Upper and lower motor neurons
questions.suggestedRationale: ALS degenerates both upper and lower motor neurons, not sensory neurons.

questions.prompt: Which statement applies to Huntington’s disease?
options: It is inherited as an autosomal recessive trait.
It is manifested in individuals by age 20 years.
It presents with choreiform movements in the upper body and decreased ability to concentrate.
It causes decreased levels of all neurotransmitters in the CNS.
questions.suggestedLabel: C. It presents with choreiform movements in the upper body and decreased ability to concentrate.
questions.suggestedRationale: Huntington disease is autosomal dominant and causes chorea plus declining concentration, usually in mid-adult life.

questions.prompt: Which of the following dietary supplements has reduced the incidence of spina bifida in recent years?
questions.suggestedLabel: B. Folic acid
questions.suggestedRationale: Folic acid supplementation has reduced the incidence of neural-tube defects such as spina bifida.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is used to confirm the diagnosis of, and classify, seizures?
options: Changes in the characteristics of cerebrospinal fluid
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Electroencephalogram
questions.suggestedRationale: EEG is used to confirm and classify seizure types.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a typical early sign of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)?
options: Weakness and muscle atrophy in upper limbs
questions.suggestedLabel: D. Weakness and muscle atrophy in upper limbs
questions.suggestedRationale: Early ALS often shows weakness and atrophy in the hands and arms; cognition and eye movements are typically spared at first.

questions.prompt: Which of the following classes of drugs may provide temporary improvement in cases of myasthenia gravis?
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Anticholinesterase agents
questions.suggestedRationale: Anticholinesterase drugs temporarily improve neuromuscular transmission in myasthenia gravis.

questions.prompt: Communicating hydrocephalus causes increased intracranial pressure because of
options: failure of the subarachnoid to absorb CSF.
obstruction in the lumbar area of the spinal cord.
scar tissue from encephalitis blocking flow of CSF.
questions.suggestedLabel: B. failure of the subarachnoid to absorb CSF.
questions.suggestedRationale: Communicating hydrocephalus is impaired CSF absorption from the subarachnoid space.

questions.prompt: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is caused by
options: inheritance of an autosomal dominant trait.
infection in the brain by HIV.
an autoimmune reaction that damages nerve receptors.
infection in the brain by a prion.
questions.suggestedLabel: D. infection in the brain by a prion.
questions.suggestedRationale: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is a prion infection of the brain.

questions.prompt: Amoebic meningoencephalitis is caused by the organism:
questions.suggestedLabel: A. Naeglaria fowleri
questions.suggestedRationale: Primary amoebic meningoencephalitis is caused by Naegleria fowleri.

questions.prompt: Which statement is TRUE about amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)?
options: Cause of death is usually a cardiac arrhythmia.
questions.suggestedLabel: A. Cognitive function remains normal.
questions.suggestedRationale: Cognition usually remains intact in ALS; death is typically from respiratory failure, not arrhythmia.
